title: Simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences
blurb: Classify any sentence by counting its independent and dependent clauses, and build the type a question asks for.
question: “When the storm hit, the power failed, and the backup generator started.” Is this sentence compound, complex or compound-complex, and what is the fastest way to prove it on the TEAS?

teach.body: Formally, a sentence's structural type depends on the number of independent clauses (subject + verb + complete thought; can stand alone) and dependent clauses (subject + verb, but introduced by a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun; cannot stand alone). Plain English: ignore length and ignore how many nouns or verbs there are. Count the clauses that could stand alone and the clauses that could not. The count names the type.

head: Type
Independent
Dependent
Example
rows: The nurse and the aide checked and recorded the vitals.
The clinic opened early, but the lab stayed closed.
Because the lab was closed, the samples waited.
When the storm hit, the power failed, and the generator started.
teach.caption: Compound subjects (the nurse and the aide) and compound verbs (checked and recorded) do not add clauses.

root.label: Any dependent clause?
root.sub: Look for because, when, although, who, which, that...

values: and, but, or, so, yet; however
because, although, when, if, who, which

rows.label: Example
values: It rained, so we stayed in.
Because it rained, we stayed in.

teach.caption: The dependent clause can come first, last or in the middle: “The patient who fell needs an X-ray” is complex.

steps.label: Mark dependents
steps.sub: Pairs led by because, when, who, that...

steps.label: Count the rest
steps.sub: Pairs that stand alone are independent

teach.body: Jordan Ellis, a nursing applicant, takes the opening question. Subject-verb pairs: storm hit, power failed, generator started. “When the storm hit” begins with a subordinating conjunction, so it is dependent. “The power failed” and “the backup generator started” can each stand alone, so there are two independent clauses. Two independent + one dependent = compound-complex.

head: Purpose
Does what
Ends with
Example
teach.caption: Purpose and structure are separate labels: “Close the door before you leave” is imperative AND complex.

teach.text: The top TEAS traps: calling a sentence with a compound verb “compound” (it is simple), missing a relative clause (who, which, that) that makes a sentence complex, and assuming a long sentence must be compound-complex. A participial phrase such as “Running to the bus” is not a clause.

items: Simple: one independent clause, even with compound subjects or verbs.
Compound: two or more independent clauses, no dependent clause.
Complex: one independent clause plus at least one dependent clause.
Compound-complex: two or more independent clauses plus at least one dependent clause.
Count clauses, not words; relative clauses (who, which, that) count as dependent.

summary: You can now classify simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences by counting independent and dependent clauses, and combine sentences into a requested type. You can also separate structure from purpose (declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory).

A.q: Which of the following is a compound sentence?
options: The nurse and the aide checked the vitals.
The nurse checked the vitals, and the aide recorded them.
The nurse checked the vitals and recorded them.
After the nurse checked the vitals, the aide recorded them.
A.why: Two independent clauses (the nurse checked; the aide recorded) are joined by a comma and “and,” with no dependent clause.

whyNot.0: A compound subject (the nurse and the aide) still makes one clause: simple.
whyNot.2: One subject with a compound verb (checked and recorded) is still one clause: simple.
whyNot.3: “After the nurse checked the vitals” is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex.

A.q: Which of the following is a complex sentence?
options: The clinic opened early, but the lab stayed closed.
The clinic opened early; the lab stayed closed.
Although the clinic opened early, the lab stayed closed.
The clinic and the lab opened early and stayed open until late.
A.why: “Although the clinic opened early” is a dependent clause attached to one independent clause.

whyNot.0: Two independent clauses joined by “but” make a compound sentence.
whyNot.1: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon make a compound sentence.
whyNot.3: This has a compound subject and compound verb but only one clause: simple.

A.q: Which of the following is a simple sentence?
options: The nurse and the aide checked and recorded the vitals.
The nurse checked the vitals, and the aide recorded them.
When the nurse checked the vitals, the aide recorded them.
The nurse checked the vitals; the aide recorded them.
A.why: There is one clause with a compound subject and a compound verb, so it is simple.

whyNot.1: Two independent clauses joined by “and” make it compound.
whyNot.2: “When the nurse checked the vitals” is a dependent clause, so it is complex.
whyNot.3: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon make it compound.

B.q: Which of the following is a compound-complex sentence?
options: When the storm hit, the power failed.
The storm hit, and the power failed.
The storm hit the coast late at night, and the power failed for hours.
When the storm hit, the power failed, and the generator started.
B.why: It has one dependent clause (When the storm hit) and two independent clauses (the power failed; the generator started).

whyNot.0: One dependent clause and only one independent clause make it complex.
whyNot.1: Two independent clauses with no dependent clause make it compound.
whyNot.2: Length does not matter: two independent clauses and no dependent clause make it compound.

B.q: What type of sentence is this? “The patient who arrived first waited the longest.”
options: Complex
Simple
Compound
Compound-complex
B.why: “Who arrived first” is a relative (dependent) clause inside one independent clause, so the sentence is complex.

whyNot.1: The relative clause “who arrived first” has its own subject and verb, so there are two clauses.
whyNot.2: There is only one independent clause; the other clause is dependent.
whyNot.3: Compound-complex needs two independent clauses; this has one.

B.q: What type of sentence is this? “Maria studied every night, yet she still felt nervous; however, she passed.”
options: Simple
Complex
Compound
Compound-complex
B.why: There are three independent clauses (Maria studied; she felt nervous; she passed) and no dependent clause, so it is compound.

whyNot.0: There are three subject-verb pairs that each stand alone, not one.
whyNot.1: “However” is a conjunctive adverb, not a subordinating conjunction, so no clause is dependent.
whyNot.3: Compound-complex needs a dependent clause, and this sentence has none.

C.q: Jordan must combine “The lab was closed.” and “The samples waited until morning.” into a complex sentence. Which choice does this?
options: The lab was closed, so the samples had to wait until morning.
Because the lab was closed, the samples waited until morning.
The lab was closed; the samples waited until morning.
The lab was closed, and the samples waited until morning.
C.why: “Because” turns the first idea into a dependent clause attached to one independent clause: complex.

whyNot.0: Two independent clauses joined by “so” make a compound sentence.
whyNot.2: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon make a compound sentence.
whyNot.3: Two independent clauses joined by “and” make a compound sentence.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a simple sentence?
options: Running to the bus, Mia dropped her badge.
Mia and Leo ran to the bus and caught it.
After lunch, Mia ran to the bus.
Mia ran to the bus after she ate lunch.
C.why: “After she ate lunch” has its own subject and verb, so it is a dependent clause: the sentence is complex.

whyNot.0: “Running to the bus” is a participial phrase, not a clause, so the sentence is simple.
whyNot.1: Compound subject and compound verb, but one clause: simple.
whyNot.2: “After lunch” is a prepositional phrase with no verb, so the sentence is simple.

C.q: Which of the following is an imperative sentence?
options: Please sign the consent form before noon.
Will you sign the consent form before noon?
You signed the consent form before noon.
What a relief that you signed the form!
C.why: An imperative sentence gives a command or request, with an implied subject (you).

whyNot.1: This asks a question, so it is interrogative.
whyNot.2: This makes a statement, so it is declarative.
whyNot.3: This expresses strong feeling, so it is exclamatory.

reteach.title: Clauses are train cars
reteach.question: Think of each clause as a train car. An engine car can run on its own; a trailer car cannot. How does the mix of cars name the train?

blocks.body: An independent clause is an engine: it can move alone. A dependent clause is a trailer: it has wheels (a subject and a verb) but needs an engine to pull it. One engine is a simple train. Two engines coupled together is compound. One engine pulling a trailer is complex. Two engines and at least one trailer is compound-complex. Passengers (extra nouns and verbs) never change the train's type.

blocks.text: A long train is not automatically compound-complex. Count the engines and trailers; ignore the passengers.

explain.body: Both have a subject and a verb. An independent clause stands alone. A dependent clause starts with a subordinating conjunction (because, when, although) or a relative pronoun (who, which, that) and cannot stand alone.

test.q: Which word group is an independent clause?
options: because the nurse arrived late
when the shift ended
the nurse arrived late
who arrived late
test.why: It has a subject and verb, is not introduced by a subordinating word, and can stand alone.

whyNot.3: The relative pronoun “who” makes the clause dependent.

explain.body: A simple sentence has one independent clause, even with compound subjects or verbs. A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses with a comma + FANBOYS or a semicolon.

rows.label: Example
values: The aide washed and dried the basin.
The aide washed it; the nurse dried it.

test.q: Which sentence about the basin is compound?
options: The aide washed and dried the basin.
The aide washed the basin; the nurse dried it.
The aide and the nurse washed the basin.
While the aide washed the basin, the nurse waited.
test.why: Two independent clauses are joined by a semicolon, with no dependent clause.

whyNot.0: One subject with a compound verb is still one clause: simple.
whyNot.2: A compound subject is still one clause: simple.
whyNot.3: “While the aide washed the basin” is dependent, so it is complex.

explain.body: A complex sentence has exactly one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. The dependent clause may come first (with a comma), last (usually no comma) or in the middle.

head: Position
Example
rows: When the doctor called, the nurse answered.
The nurse answered when the doctor called.
The nurse who answered was new.

test.q: Which sentence about the phone call is complex?
options: The doctor called, and the nurse answered.
The doctor and the nurse talked by phone.
The doctor called; the nurse answered.
The nurse answered when the doctor called.
test.why: “When the doctor called” is a dependent clause attached to one independent clause.

whyNot.0: Two independent clauses joined by “and” make it compound.
whyNot.1: One clause with a compound subject makes it simple.
whyNot.2: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon make it compound.

explain.body: A compound-complex sentence has two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. Count them separately before naming the type.

test.q: How many clauses of each kind are in this sentence? “Although the test was long, Sam finished early, and he checked his work.”
options: 2 independent, 1 dependent
1 independent, 2 dependent
2 independent, 0 dependent
3 independent, 0 dependent
test.why: “Although the test was long” is dependent; “Sam finished early” and “he checked his work” are independent. That makes it compound-complex.

whyNot.1: “He checked his work” follows “and,” a coordinating conjunction, so it is independent.
whyNot.2: “Although” makes its clause dependent, so there is one dependent clause.
whyNot.3: “Although the test was long” cannot stand alone, so it is not independent.
